title: Filtering Data: WHERE, Operators & Pattern Matching — Narration Scripts

lecture.New_Day3Part1audio01.mp3: The WHERE clause is SQL's horizontal row-level filter. The database engine evaluates the boolean expression in WHERE for every candidate row produced by FROM. Only rows that evaluate to TRUE pass through — rows that evaluate to FALSE or NULL are silently discarded.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio02.mp3: Here is the minimal WHERE clause anatomy. First, write SELECT followed by the columns you want. Then FROM the table name. Finally, WHERE followed by your condition — for example, WHERE salary is greater than eighty thousand.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio03.mp3: An important detail about execution order: WHERE runs as Step 2, after FROM but before GROUP BY, HAVING, and SELECT. This means WHERE cannot reference aliases defined in the SELECT list, because those aliases don't exist yet at filtering time.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio04.mp3: SQL provides six comparison operators for building WHERE conditions. Let's look at each one.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio05.mp3: The equals sign checks for exact match. Not equal, written as less-than greater-than, checks inequality. Greater-than and less-than work as expected for numeric ranges. Greater-than-or-equal and less-than-or-equal include the boundary value in the result set.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio06.mp3: Here are comparison operators in action. The first query retrieves employees earning more than sixty thousand. The second finds products where stock quantity is zero or less. The third uses not-equal to exclude a specific department.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio07.mp3: When you need to combine multiple conditions, SQL provides three logical operators: NOT, AND, and OR.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio08.mp3: NOT reverses a condition — NOT TRUE becomes FALSE, and NOT FALSE becomes TRUE. Use it to exclude specific values or negate complex conditions.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio09.mp3: AND returns TRUE only when both conditions are true simultaneously. A single FALSE operand makes the entire AND expression FALSE.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio10.mp3: OR returns TRUE when at least one condition is true. Both operands must be FALSE for OR to return FALSE.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio11.mp3: Operator precedence determines evaluation order: NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR. This means AND groups before OR — always use parentheses when mixing AND and OR to make your intent explicit and avoid logical bugs.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio12.mp3: Here are the logical operators in practice. The first query uses AND to find active employees in department twenty. The second uses OR to find customers in the North or South region. The third uses NOT with LIKE to exclude a naming pattern.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio13.mp3: A key warning: when NULL is involved in any comparison or logical expression, the result is UNKNOWN — not TRUE and not FALSE. Because WHERE only passes rows where the condition is strictly TRUE, NULL values are silently filtered out. Always use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to explicitly test for missing values.

questions.New_Day3Question01.mp3: Ready to filter by price? Retrieve the name and unit price of all products with a price greater than ten thousand. Sort the results by price descending.
questions.New_Day3Question01sol.mp3: Let's write this query. SELECT name, then unit_price... FROM products... WHERE unit_price is greater than 10000... ORDER BY unit_price DESC. The WHERE clause filters out all products at or below ten thousand, and ORDER BY arranges the remaining products from most expensive to least.
questions.New_Day3Question02.mp3: Time to filter by region! Retrieve first name, last name, and region for customers located in either the North or East region. Use the IN operator.
questions.New_Day3Question02sol.mp3: Here is the solution. SELECT first_name, last_name, region... FROM customers... WHERE region IN open paren 'North', 'East' close paren. The IN operator is a cleaner alternative to writing two OR conditions — it checks if region matches any value in the provided list.
questions.New_Day3Question03.mp3: Let's practice BETWEEN! Find employees earning between sixty thousand and one hundred thousand inclusive. Retrieve first name, last name, and salary.
questions.New_Day3Question03sol.mp3: Let's code this. SELECT first_name, last_name, salary... FROM employees... WHERE salary BETWEEN 60000 AND 100000. BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends — it is equivalent to writing salary greater-than-or-equal-to sixty thousand AND salary less-than-or-equal-to one hundred thousand.
questions.New_Day3Question04.mp3: Time to search with a pattern! Find all employees whose first name starts with the letter S. Retrieve first name, last name, and salary.
questions.New_Day3Question04sol.mp3: The solution uses LIKE. SELECT first_name, last_name, salary... FROM employees... WHERE first_name LIKE 'S%'. The percent wildcard matches any sequence of characters — so 'S%' means: any name starting with S, followed by zero or more characters.
questions.New_Day3Question05.mp3: Let's combine two conditions with AND! Find active employees — where is_active equals one — who are in department twenty. Retrieve first name, department id, and salary.
questions.New_Day3Question05sol.mp3: Here is the query. SELECT first_name, department_id, salary... FROM employees... WHERE is_active = 1 AND department_id = 20. Both conditions must be true for a row to pass. AND is the right operator here because we want employees who are simultaneously active AND in department twenty.
questions.New_Day3Question06.mp3: Final challenge — NULL handling! Find all employees who have no commission assigned. Retrieve first name, last name, and commission.
questions.New_Day3Question06sol.mp3: The solution uses IS NULL. SELECT first_name, last_name, commission... FROM employees... WHERE commission IS NULL. Critical point: you cannot write commission equals NULL — that always returns UNKNOWN and filters every row out. IS NULL is the only correct way to check for missing values in SQL.
